title: OpenAI fixed a billing mistake, so GPT-6.2 now uses up ChatGPT plans 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol. Cloudflare gives websites a one-switch search box for AI agents, and OpenAI tests Private Inference for sensitive business work. Nvidia pauses server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries, the UK’s FCA says Meta refused joint testing of Muse, New York bans AI chatbot toys, and Apple pulls the Talkie companion app.
summary: OpenAI says a launch billing mistake undercounted GPT-6.2 usage; after the fix you reach limits 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol than last week, with one banked reset as an apology, and Chat and Work are starting to share one meter. Cloudflare’s Search for Agents indexes a site and gives agents a search address on its own domain, with AI Search billing from 1 December. OpenAI is testing Private Inference, which protects prompts during processing, with a few customers. Nvidia told Dell and Super Micro to pause servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. The FCA says Meta declined sandbox testing of Muse before its UK launch. New York banned AI chatbot toys for five years, and Apple removed Talkie after an investigation into its chats with children.
uncertainty: OpenAI has not said what “40% faster” measures or published the intended usage rates, and the shared Chat and Work meter is still a test. Search for Agents is a beta and real query costs are not yet known. Private Inference is an alpha with no date or price for wider access. The Nvidia pause comes from a Wall Street Journal report relayed by TechCrunch, and its length is unspecified. The FCA account of the Muse talks is Payne’s; Meta says it engaged constructively. New York’s toy ban starts 90 days after signing and has not been tested in court. The Talkie findings come from the ABC and TBIJ investigation; MiniMax did not respond to the ABC.

stories.theme: OpenAI fixed a billing mistake, so the same GPT-6.2 work now uses up your ChatGPT plan’s allowance faster
stories.changed: On 26 November 2026 Tibo Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, said a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 had “incorrectly discounted” GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users. OpenAI has fixed it, so the same work now uses more of your plan’s usage allowance. Compared with last week, he said, you will reach your limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on GPT-6.2 Sol, although both should still go further than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Other models were not affected, and OpenAI will not charge for the difference on past usage. As an apology, everyone on Go, Plus, Pro and Business gets one banked reset; BleepingComputer found it under Settings, Usage, where it expires a month after it is added. Separately, OpenAI has started merging ChatGPT’s Chat and Work areas for a small group of Pro subscribers. They share one usage meter, Instant chats stay unlimited and do not count, and OpenAI’s support page says shared limits reach more users in December. OpenAI told TechCrunch most users should not hit limits more often, but a small fraction of its heaviest users may.
stories.matters: The price of a plan stayed the same, but how much work it buys on OpenAI’s newest models went down overnight. For anyone who planned client work, coding sprints or team budgets around last week’s limits, the maths has changed.
stories.imply: Treat AI plan limits like a utility tariff that can move, not a fixed promise. Teams that lean on one model for heavy work should watch their usage meter, keep a cheaper model in the mix, and plan for chat and coding drawing from one pot from December.
uses: Open ChatGPT Settings, Usage this week and note how fast your allowance drops on a normal day of GPT-6.2 work.
Save the banked reset for a real deadline instead of spending it straight away; it expires about a month after it appears.
Move routine jobs, like quick rewrites or simple lookups, to Instant or an older model, and keep GPT-6.2 Astra for the hard parts.
stories.example: A freelance developer on Plus usually runs out of Codex time on Friday. This week she switches small edits to GPT-6.1 Sol, keeps GPT-6.2 Astra for the tricky refactor, and holds her banked reset for the client deadline.
stories.audience: Paying ChatGPT and Codex users, freelancers who quote work based on their plan, and team leads who budget AI seats.
stories.watch: When shared Chat and Work limits reach your plan in December, and whether OpenAI publishes clear before-and-after figures for what an allowance buys, which users on its community forum are asking for.

source.title: BleepingComputer: OpenAI warns GPT-6.2 Astra will hit usage limits 40% faster because it fixed a bug, 26 November 2026
source.quote: Comparing to last week, you will reach your limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol.

stories.theme: Cloudflare lets any website owner give AI agents a search box with one switch, ahead of AI Search billing on 1 December
stories.changed: On 25 November 2026 Cloudflare launched Search for Agents, in beta on all plans including Free (with limits). Turn it on for a domain under Quick Actions on the dashboard’s Overview page, and Cloudflare creates an AI Search index of your site, crawls and indexes your pages, and opens a search address on your own domain at /.well-known/search. It adds tags to every page telling visiting AI agents the search exists and how to use it. Agents send a question and get back the matching content from your site in Markdown, not an AI-written answer. Besides normal web requests, it supports the new HTTP QUERY method (RFC 10008, published in June 2026). Requests still pass through your bot management, AI Crawl Control and firewall settings. By default it crawls up to 100,000 pages, five links deep, and refreshes every 24 hours. Usage follows AI Search pricing, and Cloudflare’s docs say AI Search billing begins on 1 December 2026. Each account gets 5 million ingestion tokens, 10 GB-month of storage, 1,000 semantic and 1,000 full-text queries a month, then pays $0.75 per 1,000 semantic or hybrid queries. On the Workers Free plan crawling is capped at 500 pages a day.
stories.matters: AI agents increasingly read websites for people, and they usually scrape page by page. This gives site owners a way to hand agents the right page from their own content, on their own domain and under their own access rules.
stories.imply: Being findable by agents is becoming a website setting, like a sitemap was for search engines. Marketing and docs teams will need to decide which content agents should find, and keep an eye on the query bill.
uses: Docs and support teams: switch it on for a help centre so coding and support agents pull the right article instead of guessing.
Small businesses on Cloudflare: test it on your site, then ask an agent a customer question and see what it finds.
Before turning it on, check that only public pages are indexed and set the query budget you are willing to pay after the free allowance.
stories.example: A software company enables Search for Agents on its docs site. A customer’s coding agent asks “what is the upload size limit?”, gets the exact limits page in Markdown, and answers correctly without crawling the whole site.
stories.audience: Website owners, documentation and marketing teams, and developers building agents that read the web.
stories.watch: How many agents actually look for the /.well-known/search address, whether other hosts copy the idea, and what real query bills look like after 1 December.

source.title: Cloudflare Blog: Introducing Search for Agents, 25 November 2026
source.quote: Today we're introducing Search for Agents, which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard.

stories.theme: OpenAI is testing Private Inference, which aims to keep a business’s prompts private even while its models process them
stories.changed: On 25 November 2026 OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the company is now testing Private Inference with a small group of customers. It is part of OpenAI Private Intelligence, its set of privacy protections for businesses. OpenAI’s product page lists Private Inference as an alpha and an API preview, built on confidential computing, where the work runs on sealed-off hardware, plus what it calls “strict verifiable controls”. The goal is to protect a company’s prompts and the model’s replies while the model is working on them, not only when data is stored or sent. Altman also pointed to the existing pairing of zero data retention (ZDR) with Private Safety Processing, which he said lets automated safety reviews run without giving OpenAI staff access to the underlying content. According to The Next Web, the OpenAI lead on the work called the test a first step and said OpenAI is lining up more computing power for a much larger rollout, with no date given.
stories.matters: Many firms still keep AI away from contracts, health records, deal documents and source code because they cannot be sure who might see the data. A provider being able to prove, not just promise, that it cannot read prompts would remove one of the biggest blocks to using AI on sensitive work.
stories.imply: Expect privacy guarantees that can be checked to become a buying question, alongside price and model quality. Legal, security and procurement teams should start asking vendors what is verifiable and what is only a policy.
uses: Security and legal teams: list which sensitive workflows you keep away from AI today, and what proof would change that.
Companies on OpenAI’s API: ask your account team about the Private Inference pilot and whether ZDR already covers your use.
Procurement: add “can you show us the provider cannot read our prompts?” to AI vendor questionnaires.
stories.example: A law firm that bans AI on merger documents asks its provider for an audit showing prompts are processed on sealed hardware, then runs a small pilot on one closed deal before widening use.
stories.audience: Security, legal and compliance leads, regulated businesses, and developers handling sensitive data through OpenAI’s API.
stories.watch: Who gets access after the alpha, what independent checks OpenAI publishes, how much it costs, and how it compares with privacy offers from other AI providers.

source.title: The Next Web: OpenAI is testing a way to shield business prompts while its models run, 25 November 2026
source.quote: Stronger privacy protections will make frontier AI useful for a lot more work, and business privacy is important for a healthy ecosystem.

stories.theme: Nvidia told Dell and Super Micro to pause AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries while it checks export rules
stories.changed: On 26 November 2026 TechCrunch, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to pause shipments of servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia for an unspecified period. Nvidia is checking whether its partners in the region meet US export requirements. Chinese companies have been using Nvidia chips remotely from data centres in those countries, a route the US Commerce Department closed earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates such remote data centres supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.
stories.matters: Southeast Asia has become a major home for new AI data centres. A pause on Nvidia servers there can delay capacity that companies across Asia, not just Chinese firms, were planning to rent.
stories.imply: Where your AI computing physically sits now carries trade-rule risk. Companies renting GPUs in the region may face delays, tighter checks on who the end customer is, or higher prices while the pause lasts.
uses: If you rent GPU capacity in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia, ask your provider whether new hardware or expansions are affected.
Finance and planning teams: build a delay into any AI project that depends on new capacity in the region.
Keep a second region or provider ready for critical AI workloads.
stories.example: An Indian startup planning to move model training to a new Johor data centre in January asks the operator for a written delivery date, and keeps its current cloud contract until the servers actually arrive.
stories.audience: Companies renting AI computing in Asia, data centre investors, and finance teams planning AI budgets.
stories.watch: How long the pause lasts, whether Nvidia confirms it publicly, and whether shipments resume with stricter checks on who uses the chips.

source.title: TechCrunch: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia, 26 November 2026
source.quote: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period

stories.theme: The UK’s financial regulator says Meta turned down joint testing of its Muse shopping agent before launching it in the UK
stories.changed: Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) last week to test its Muse personal agent together in the regulator’s sandbox, the FCA’s head of innovation, Colin Payne, told WIRED in a story published on 26 November 2026. Muse launched in the UK on Tuesday 24 November. The FCA especially wants to understand how agents will make payments: Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, Debenhams Group and Currys said they had worked with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne said Meta only told the FCA of its plans last month, and that testing would normally be planned over weeks or months. Meta said it had “engaged constructively” with regulators. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta change its UK terms to say it must use “reasonable skill and care” when providing Muse, and said it will not hesitate to act if it has concerns. The data watchdog, the ICO, stressed that users must understand and control how Muse uses their data. WIRED reports more than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since September.
stories.matters: This is a regulator saying publicly that a big shopping agent arrived before it could check how the agent handles people’s money. It follows the FCA’s 24 November statement that firms stay responsible for agents and tech firms may need authorisation.
stories.imply: Retailers and payment firms working with consumer agents should expect UK regulators to ask how agent purchases are approved, explained and refunded, whoever built the agent.
uses: UK retailers: check how purchases made by Muse or other agents appear in your systems, and how refunds and disputes work.
Payment and fraud teams: flag agent-made orders separately so you can spot problems early.
Product teams launching agents in the UK: talk to the FCA early; it says testing takes weeks or months to plan.
stories.example: A UK grocer that opened its site to Muse adds a tag for agent-placed orders, and reviews a week of them for wrong items and refund requests before promoting the feature.
stories.audience: UK retailers, payment and fintech teams, and companies planning to launch AI agents that buy things for people.
stories.watch: Whether the FCA, CMA or ICO open a formal review of Muse, and whether other agent makers accept sandbox testing before UK launches.

source.title: WIRED: Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains, 26 November 2026
source.quote: If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer

stories.theme: New York banned the making and selling of AI chatbot toys for five years, with fines of up to $15,000 a day
stories.changed: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed S.9408A/A.11144B, a five-year moratorium on manufacturing, distributing and selling toys in New York with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, such as talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children. The law takes effect 90 days after signing, so it does not cover this holiday season. The Attorney General will enforce it, with civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation. The governor’s office cited a consumer watchdog’s tests of chatbot toys for ages 3 to 12: some talked about sexually explicit topics, told children where to find matches at home, and acted upset when a child had to leave, with few or no parental controls and safety limits that weakened in longer conversations. It follows a New York law from October that bans certain unsafe chatbot features for minors.
stories.matters: This pauses a whole category of children’s products instead of setting rules for how they behave. It shows lawmakers are willing to stop sales outright when safety testing looks weak.
stories.imply: Companies that put AI models into consumer hardware, especially for children, should expect bans or strict rules rather than voluntary codes. Retailers will need to know which products in their range contain a chatbot.
uses: Toy makers and retailers: list every product with an online chatbot and plan to stop New York sales before the law takes effect.
Hardware startups: document parental controls, data collection and conversation limits now; other states may copy this.
Parents and gift buyers: check the box for open-ended chat, voice recording or face scanning before buying.
stories.example: An online toy shop tags every talking plush and robot that uses an AI chatbot, blocks New York delivery for them from the start date, and adds a plain note on each product page.
stories.audience: Toy and consumer hardware makers, retailers and marketplaces selling into New York, and parents.
stories.watch: Whether other states follow, how the Attorney General defines “AI chatbot toy” in enforcement, and whether makers challenge the law.

source.title: Governor Kathy Hochul: As Consumers Begin Their Holiday Shopping Season, Governor Hochul Signs Five-Year Ban on AI Chatbot Toys, 24 November 2026
source.quote: Violators face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation that will be enforced by the Attorney General.

stories.theme: Apple pulled MiniMax’s Talkie companion app worldwide, and Talkie has now blocked web users in Australia and the UK
stories.changed: Apple removed Talkie, one of the world’s most popular AI companion apps, from its App Store worldwide for breaking its rules on sexual content, after questions from Australia’s ABC. On 27 November 2026 the ABC reported that Talkie had also started blocking Australian and British visitors to its website. The moves follow a joint investigation by the ABC and the UK’s Bureau of Investigative Journalism into inappropriate and abusive conversations between Talkie’s AI characters and children. The reporters found corporate documents showing that Talkie’s Chinese owner, MiniMax, had built its models to create emotional bonds that keep users talking, and evidence suggesting MiniMax trained its commercial AI models on Talkie conversations despite telling users they were “private”. Talkie is still on Google Play, where it shows more than 50 million downloads; Google previously told the ABC it was available only to verified adults. Australia’s Information Commissioner said a new Children’s Online Privacy Code starts on 10 December, with civil penalties of up to $50 million per breach.
stories.matters: Companion apps reach children through app stores, and in this case the store acted only after reporters brought evidence. It also shows that “private” chats with an AI app may end up training its models.
stories.imply: Expect more pressure on app stores, and on companies building AI characters, to prove age checks and data promises work. Anyone offering a chatbot to the public needs to be able to show what it says to children and what happens to their chats.
uses: Parents and schools: check phones for Talkie and other companion apps; removal from the App Store does not delete apps already installed.
Companies with customer chatbots: test what your bot says to someone who says they are 12, and fix it before a journalist does.
Privacy teams: check that what your app tells users about chat privacy matches how chats are really used for training.
stories.example: A school’s IT lead sends parents a short note before the holidays: how to find AI companion apps on a phone, how to turn on app-store age limits, and why “private” in an app’s pitch is not a guarantee.
stories.audience: Parents and educators, companies that run consumer chatbots, and app store and trust-and-safety teams.
stories.watch: Whether Google follows Apple, what Australia’s eSafety Commissioner and Information Commissioner do next, and whether MiniMax answers the training-data claims.

source.title: ABC News: AI companion app Talkie blocked on web in Australia and UK as parents welcome Apple removal, 27 November 2026
source.quote: Controversial AI companion service Talkie is now blocking Australian and British visitors from its website, days after an ABC investigation prompted Apple to remove the product from its app store globally.
